options.text: The removal of undigested food from the body
The transport of food through the body
The absorption of nutrients into the blood
The breakdown of large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed

questions.explanation: Digestion is the breakdown of large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood and used by cells. It involves both mechanical digestion (chewing, churning) and chemical digestion (enzymes breaking bonds).

options.text: No — bile is a type of acid
Yes — bile is a lipase enzyme
No — bile emulsifies fats (breaks them into smaller droplets) but does not chemically digest them; it is not an enzyme
Yes — bile is a protease enzyme

questions.explanation: Bile is NOT an enzyme. It is produced by the liver, stored in the gallbladder, and released into the small intestine. Bile salts emulsify fats — they break large fat globules into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase to act on. Bile also neutralises stomach acid, creating the alkaline conditions needed for intestinal enzymes.

questions.stem: What does amylase break down and what are the products?
questions.explanation: Amylase is a carbohydrase enzyme that breaks down starch into maltose. It is produced in the salivary glands (begins starch digestion in the mouth) and the pancreas (continues in the small intestine). Maltase then breaks maltose into glucose.

questions.stem: At what pH does pepsin work best, and where in the body does it function?
questions.explanation: Pepsin is a protease enzyme that works in the stomach at an optimum pH of about 2 (very acidic). This acidic environment is maintained by hydrochloric acid (HCl) secreted by cells in the stomach lining. Pancreatic proteases (like trypsin) work in the small intestine at pH 7-8.

options.text: Lipids (fats) into fatty acids and glycerol

questions.explanation: Lipase breaks down lipids (fats and oils) into fatty acids and glycerol. It is produced mainly by the pancreas and works in the small intestine. Bile salts emulsify fats first, increasing the surface area available for lipase to act on, speeding up digestion.

questions.stem: How are the villi in the small intestine adapted for efficient absorption?

options.text: They have a large surface area (finger-like projections with microvilli), a thin wall (one cell thick), a good blood supply, and lacteals for fat absorption
They are very thick to slow down food movement
They produce enzymes to digest food
They are found only in the stomach

questions.explanation: Villi are adapted for absorption with: a very large surface area (millions of finger-like projections, each covered in microvilli), walls only one cell thick (short diffusion distance), an extensive network of blood capillaries (maintains a concentration gradient for glucose and amino acids), and lacteals (absorb fatty acids and glycerol).

questions.stem: What is the main function of the large intestine?

options.text: Absorption of glucose and amino acids
Absorption of water from undigested food, forming faeces

questions.explanation: The large intestine (colon) absorbs water and some minerals from the remaining undigested food material, forming semi-solid faeces. The large intestine also contains bacteria that produce some vitamins (like vitamin K). Faeces are stored in the rectum before being egested through the anus.

questions.stem: Which food test uses iodine solution?
questions.explanation: Iodine solution tests for starch. Add iodine solution to the food sample — if starch is present, the colour changes from brown/yellow to blue-black. Benedict's tests for reducing sugars (heat required), Biuret tests for proteins, and ethanol emulsion or Sudan III tests for lipids.

questions.stem: What deficiency disease is caused by a lack of vitamin C?
questions.explanation: Scurvy is caused by a deficiency of vitamin C, which is needed for collagen production. Symptoms include bleeding gums, bruising, poor wound healing, and joint pain. Rickets is caused by a lack of vitamin D (weak bones). Anaemia can be caused by a lack of iron. Kwashiorkor is caused by severe protein deficiency.

questions.stem: What is the difference between mechanical and chemical digestion?

options.text: Mechanical digestion uses enzymes; chemical digestion uses teeth
Mechanical digestion only occurs in the stomach; chemical digestion only in the mouth
Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces (teeth, churning); chemical digestion uses enzymes to break chemical bonds in food molecules

questions.explanation: Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces without changing it chemically — e.g., chewing (teeth), churning (stomach muscles). This increases the surface area for enzymes to act on. Chemical digestion uses enzymes to break the chemical bonds in large food molecules, producing smaller, soluble molecules.
